chunks: From him, from Usman ibn Isa, from Sama'ah who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about the man who begins with the man in the letter. He (peace be upon him) said: There is no problem with it. That is from the preference (generosity/honor) that the man begins with his brother to honour him.
ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to write the recipient's name before the sender's name in a letter according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Recorded in *Al-Kafi*, this hadith clarifies that initiating a letter by naming the recipient is not only permissible but considered an act of *fadl* (generosity/honor), reflecting the cultural etiquette of prioritizing the esteemed addressee. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) links this epistolary custom to the broader Islamic virtue of honoring one's brother, demonstrating how social manners are elevated to spiritual significance in Shia jurisprudence. This ruling underscores the flexibility of *adab* (etiquette) in communication, allowing for expressions of respect that strengthen communal bonds.

en.hubeali: From him, from Usman Bin Isa, from Sama’at who said,

‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> about the man who begins with the (name of the recipient) man in the letter. He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘There is no problem with it. That is from the preference that the man begins with (the name of) his brother to honour him’.
en.sarwar: 5. It is narrated from him (narrator of the Hadith above) from ‘Uthman ibn ‘Isa from Sama’a who has said the following: “Once I asked abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) about a man who initiates writing to another man. The Imam said, ‘It is not an offense. It is an excellent act when a man initiates honoring his brother (in belief).”’
